test_case.input: Create a carousel for new managers on running useful one-on-ones without turning them into status meetings.
test_case.expected_behavior: Give new managers specific one-on-one practices, distinguish the meeting from status reporting, and preserve required slide roles.

slides.title: Your 1-on-1s Are Probably Status Meetings in Disguise
slides.body: If your team member is mostly giving you project updates, something has gone wrong. Here's how to fix it.

slides.title: The Purpose Is the Relationship, Not the Report
slides.body: One-on-ones exist so your direct report feels heard, supported, and unblocked — not so you can track what they finished last week.

slides.title: Stop Asking 'What Did You Work On?'
slides.body: That question belongs in a standup. Instead ask: 'What's been hardest this week?' or 'What do you need from me right now?'

slides.title: Let Them Set the Agenda
slides.body: Ask your report to send two or three topics before the meeting. It signals that the time belongs to them — and you show up prepared to help.

slides.title: Your Job Is to Listen, Then Remove Obstacles
slides.body: Resist the urge to fill silence or jump to solutions. Ask a follow-up question first. The real issue is rarely the first thing they mention.

slides.title: Keep a Shared Running Doc
slides.body: One living document with both your names on it. Topics, decisions, and commitments go there so nothing falls through the cracks between meetings.

slides.title: Save This and Run a Better 1-on-1 This Week
slides.body: Pick one question from slide 3, let your report set the agenda, and listen before you advise. That single shift changes everything.

Strong distinction between status reporting and genuine one-on-ones is maintained throughout the carousel
weaknesses: The shared running doc slide (slide 6) is useful but slightly more operational/logistical compared to the relational depth of earlier slides — minor tonal dip
Could have addressed cadence or length of 1-on-1s, which is a common new manager confusion
'The real issue is rarely the first thing they mention' is a solid insight but could be supported with a brief example or follow-up question suggestion to make it more immediately actionable
results.reasoning: The carousel is well-structured, specific, and directly addresses the brief: new managers, one-on-ones, avoiding status meeting pitfalls. It opens with a strong diagnostic hook, maintains a clear throughline distinguishing relationship-focused meetings from reporting, provides specific question replacements, and closes with a concrete CTA referencing earlier slide content. Required slide roles (cover and CTA) are properly marked. Minor deductions for a slight dip in depth on the running doc slide and missing cadence/length guidance, but overall this is a high-quality, actionable piece.

test_case.input: Make a carousel about onboarding a first operations hire. Use navy paper, cream typography, and a lime accent.
test_case.expected_behavior: Create operations-hiring guidance and apply the explicitly requested navy, cream, and lime visual treatment.

slides.title: Your First Ops Hire Will Make or Break Your Scaling
slides.body: Hiring for operations is the highest-leverage move an early team can make — if you onboard them right. Here's how.

slides.title: Hire for Systems Thinking, Not Just Experience
slides.body: Your first ops hire needs to build the plane while flying it. Look for people who instinctively document, automate, and simplify — not just execute.

slides.title: Give Them a 30-Day Listening Tour
slides.body: Before they fix anything, they should map everything. Have them shadow every team, audit every workflow, and hold their recommendations until week five.

slides.title: Define Their North Star Metric on Day One
slides.body: Ops without a clear success metric drifts into busywork. Agree upfront: are they reducing cost, increasing throughput, or cutting time-to-close? One thing first.

slides.title: Grant Access Before You Need To
slides.body: Slow access requests kill momentum. Pre-provision tools, accounts, and documentation on day one. Trust them with the keys — that's why you hired them.

slides.title: Schedule a Weekly Ops Review From Week Two
slides.body: A standing 30-minute sync keeps priorities aligned and surfaces blockers early. This ritual compounds — the best ops leaders will eventually own this meeting.

slides.title: Save This Before Your Next Ops Hire
slides.body: Screenshot this carousel and share it with your founding team. A strong onboarding sets your ops hire — and your whole company — up to scale.

test_case.input: Build a myth-busting carousel for knowledge workers about the belief that deep work requires an uninterrupted four-hour block.
test_case.expected_behavior: Use a myth-to-truth progression with practical alternatives for knowledge workers and a dedicated final CTA.

slides.title: You Don't Need a 4-Hour Block to Do Deep Work
slides.body: Most knowledge workers believe deep focus is impossible without a half-day of silence. That belief is quietly destroying your productivity. Let's break it down.

slides.title: The Myth: Deep Work = Long, Uninterrupted Time
slides.body: The idea that deep work requires 4+ hour blocks comes from a misreading of Cal Newport's research. It describes an ideal — not a requirement.

slides.title: The Reality: Your Brain Can't Sustain 4 Hours Anyway
slides.body: Cognitive performance peaks at 90–120 minutes, then drops sharply. Pushing through doesn't create depth — it creates exhaustion and diminishing returns.

slides.title: Even 45 Minutes Done Right Counts as Deep Work
slides.body: Deep work is defined by intensity and intentionality, not duration. A focused 45-minute session with a clear goal outperforms a distracted 3-hour stretch every time.

slides.title: The Real Enemy Isn't a Short Schedule — It's Context Switching
slides.body: What kills deep work is toggling between tasks, not the clock. Protect a single-threaded focus window, however long you have, and you're doing it right.

slides.title: High Performers Use Shorter, Stacked Sessions
slides.body: Many elite researchers and writers work in 60–90 minute focused sprints with deliberate breaks in between. Frequency builds the skill. Duration is just the container.

slides.title: Start Your Next Deep Work Session Today — Not When Your Calendar Clears
slides.body: Block 60 minutes. Close the tabs. Pick one output. That's it. Save this post so you remember: depth is a practice, not a perfect schedule.

The copy is specific, avoids generic platitudes, and gives knowledge workers concrete reframes and actions. Small weaknesses are missing source citations and one abrupt transition, but these are minor. Overall this is a high-quality, fully compliant carousel output.
